newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT- Flattening trend challenged in futures.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT- Flattening trend challenged in futures.

text.p: As the spread between two- and 30-year U.S. Treasurys flattened this week, bracing for higher interest rates ahead, some traders observed the opposite effect in futures.

The yield curve flattened as the market factored in rising expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike next week. However, the futures market instead saw a bias toward steepening trades, traders said.

As spread activity increased in general, the bias in futures toward selling the long end and buying shorter-term contracts may have resulted from traders hedging or exiting previously established flattening trades, said Kurt Fraim, Treasury futures analyst for Aubrey G. Lanston & Co.

Those market participants also may be taking a contrarian view to the growing consensus that a decision by the Federal Open Market Committee to raise short-term rates Tuesday would escalate the flattening trend, Fraim said.
The spread between the two-year Treasury note and the long bond has moved to about a 70-basis-point differential currently from 79 basis points on Wednesday, analysts said.

A flattening bias is typical of a higher-yield environment and has coincided with periods of rising yields 85 percent of the time in the past 10 years, said James Bianco, director of research at Arbor Trading Group in Barrington, Ill.
Bianco said the short end was playing catch-up this week after prices had stubbornly resisted following the long end lower.

Initial resistance to the flattening trend at the short end may have reflected a lack of urgency among institutional investors to sell short-term instruments whose purchases were financed at significantly lower rates in Japan and Switzerland, Bianco said.

Traders were watching for whether the 70-basis-point spread between two- and 30-year when-issued Treasurys would hold as support, Fraim said. A breach of that level could be viewed as confirmation of the flattening trend, he said.
Further support is pegged at the October 1995 low of 64 basis points and the March 1995 low of 61 basis points, according to MCM Moneywatch.
